name: Close the Third Frontier
description: Consent has been given and the transition has run its course. Avian's regiments will enter the common army, its courts the common system of appeals, and its towns the same political country as their neighbours. The treaty becomes a constitution in practice.

name: The First Common Budget
description: The border disappeared from the map before it disappeared from the ledgers. Two offices pay for one school, while neither accepts responsibility for the next. The government must decide who spends the common revenue and who answers to those who supplied it.

name: Citizens Beyond the Old Seals
description: A subject of the neighbouring House is no longer a foreigner, yet the clerk still demands a special fee. The old courts disagree over inheritance, debt and the right to practise a trade. One shared coat of arms is not enough: residents need dependable protection on both sides of the former border.

name: Homes Beyond the Former Border
description: Hired workers sleep in workshop annexes while empty estate houses stand boarded up for years. Municipal builders will receive contracts for homes, wells and drains. The return to ordinary life must reach beyond the main square.

name: Treatment Without a Ducal Certificate
description: Patients are asked where they came from, then sent to another district for a certificate. Physicians propose common sanitary rules, recognition of training and a shared supply list for rural clinics. Disease never respected the borders, even when the dukes did.

name: Roads to a Common Market
description: Roads once led to checkpoints and garrisons rather than neighbouring towns. Carriers now mark damaged bridges, dangerous slopes and needless detours on a single map. Their markings will become the first common road plan.

name: Machine Shops Instead of Tollhouses
description: The old customs warehouses stand beside useful roads but hold little beyond broken barriers. Craftsgriffons propose machine tools and repair shops. Orders will connect suppliers from different districts, turning the removal of the border into the beginning of new work.

name: One Drawing for Different Workshops
description: A bolt made in one district will not fit a nut from another. Masters regard their own measurements as part of their craft's dignity. A common standards office will leave their makers' marks intact, but insist that parts fit without a file.

name: Evening Classes
description: A new school will not help an adult read a contract if its doors open only during working hours. Teachers and workshops will arrange evening lessons. Their pupils have tired claws and too much experience to be ashamed of their first page.

name: The Verenian Institute of Applied Studies
description: Each former capital has its teachers, workshops and collection of instruments. Separately they request the same books and fail to finish the same experiments. A shared institute will begin with exchanged equipment, open admissions and the right to argue with a colleague from another House.

name: Serving One Country
description: Regimental rolls still remember whom the militia once assembled to fight. Common service requires more than a new cockade: shared appointments, training and accountability to civil government. Officers must decide what will sustain the defence of a small country.

name: Reserves of the Common Country
description: The old arsenals were designed for a short campaign over a neighbouring hill. The common country needs repair stocks, dispersed depots and workshops able to replace a lost delivery. An order cannot make us a great power, but we need not depend on a single road.

name: An Account to All Verenia
description: The first common projects are complete. Not every letter to the capital is grateful: contractors dispute prices, communities dispute priorities and treasurers dispute missing receipts. A published account must name both the promises fulfilled and those paid for work left undone.

name: The Country the Morning After
description: Unification will be remembered for its speeches and raised flag. Its durability will be decided later: whether medicine reaches a village, a diploma is recognised in the next town, and a court hears a complaint against its own official. We need a country that keeps working when the celebration is over.

name: The Price of Victory
description: Vincent's supporters speak readily of the inheritance victory will bring. They speak less often of the farms that must sustain it and the promises the duke will owe afterwards. Choosing this campaign means abandoning the negotiated settlement with Eyrie: Verenia is to be united by force, and Erie will have to govern the consequences. Officers, suppliers and patrons must state what they expect before the first regiment marches.

name: Promises in Writing
description: A campaign draws on credit as well as courage. Carriers advance their wagons, suppliers reserve their stock, and influential households expect their service to count when rewards are considered. Vincent will require clear undertakings and a supply service capable of keeping them. Loyalty deserves an answer; it cannot be allowed to write its own unlimited claim upon the defeated.

name: Not a Dowry
description: Rosaline Erie of Bantry has discovered that her name makes a convenient ending to other people's speeches. A union between Houses, they suggest, could be made complete through her. She intends to speak for herself. Vincent must hear her objection before anyone turns a personal correspondence into a marriage settlement or presents another griffon's future as part of the spoils.

name: The Final Ultimatum
description: Vincent will put Erie's claim behind a final demand upon Eyrie. The document cannot make his inheritance more certain than Iovinus's, but it can prepare the grounds on which he intends to fight. Existing promises of peace must still be honoured. Sending the demand leaves the decision to begin a war, and responsibility for that decision, with the duke.

name: Terms for the Defeated
description: The military result is settled. Now the people of the defeated districts must discover what Vincent's victory means at a workshop door or in a dispute over a field. Local charters could protect rights his own followers must respect. Ducal commissioners could instead organise the settlement under his direct authority. Either course will make demands that a proclamation of triumph can conceal only briefly.

name: The Districts' Own Rights
description: A promise of local rights must be usable by someone who opposed Erie. Let the districts retain recognised procedures for their property, public works and complaints, with obligations the duke's officers must also observe. Building through these institutions will take patience. It will give a town reason to repair its future without first finding a patron at Vincent's court.

name: The Duke's Commissioners
description: Vincent will place reconstruction under commissioners who answer directly to him. They can bring scattered industrial work into a common programme and make orders reach their destination quickly. Their authority will also make every intrusion the duke's own. The defeated districts may comply without feeling represented, and efficiency will have to bear the weight of that distinction.

name: The First Petition
description: A family from the defeated districts claims an estate sought by one of Vincent's wartime patrons. The patron can prove his service; the family can produce evidence that its property was never his to receive. The first difficult hearing will reveal whether the new order can distinguish a debt owed by the duke from a debt imposed on someone else.

name: Work Beyond the Victory Parade
description: The estate decision has travelled further than its authors expected. Builders and workshop owners now judge new offers against what they have learned about the settlement. Put civilian investment behind the reconstruction contracts and give industrial specialists work worth improving. A durable peace requires people to risk their savings on something other than the favour of the next victorious officer.

name: A Levy That Can Be Maintained
description: Wartime service cannot remain a succession of personal bargains. Establish regular training and reliable equipment for the troops, with obligations that can be understood beyond a patron's household. The men who fought for Erie need to know what their service now requires. The districts expected to sustain them need an answer more definite than the continuation of an emergency.

name: Reconcile the Civil Registers
description: The victorious court cannot govern two duchies from incompatible tax rolls and contradictory property registers. Surveyors, clerks and engineers will reconcile the records before the new administration claims the right to speak for every district.

name: A Duke Bound by His Word
description: Vincent will make the district guarantees binding upon his own rule. If he protected his patron's estate award, that exception must now be withdrawn and the claim returned to an evidentiary hearing. Where he already upheld the hearing, its principle must endure beyond one case. The charters can become the foundation of his settlement only if they reach the hand that signed them.

name: A Single Chancery
description: Bring the commissioners into a lasting ducal administration. Industry and the army will answer through a common chain, giving Vincent greater power to carry his decisions through. The estate judgement already made will remain part of that order. Central authority can protect a fair hearing or preserve a patron's advantage; it makes the duke responsible for whichever precedent he keeps.

name: What the Next Generation Receives
description: The children growing up under Vincent's settlement will inherit more than the story of a battle. They will inherit the answer given to a dispossessed family, the limits placed on a supporter and the habits of the offices that govern them. Let the old military rivalry end without pretending that victory has erased its consequences or decided Avian's future.

name: The Third Banner
description: Avian's council has chosen true neutrality and rejected the work between the giants. Vincent's settlement with Eyrie leaves that frontier outside the common country. His commanders propose a campaign to bring Avian into the same realm. This is a new hostile demand, not a right secretly awarded by a family treaty. Existing pacts must be honoured or ended openly.

name: The Avian Articles
description: An Avian registrar arrives with the old assessments and a list of families whose property has already been promised to two different officers. Vincent has heard this dispute before. The third House must receive a settlement it can actually live under: protected local courts and property, or a commission for which the duke accepts direct responsibility. Victory does not choose between them.

name: A Third Seat at the Table
description: The first Avian accounts have survived comparison with the treasury's ledgers. Workshops have contracts and the courts know where their decisions must be sent. Vincent can now abolish the provisional frontier and give these obligations the force of ordinary government. The third seat at his table represents inhabitants who must be governed, not merely another defeated name.

name: The Price of Vigilance
description: Iovinus Eyrie has made readiness a condition of survival. Yet the same emergency orders are renewed, the same villages supply the men, and the same returns promise soldiers an inspection cannot always find. Before choosing accommodation with Erie or a campaign to break its claim, the duke must discover what his vigilance has cost the country, and what his army can actually deliver.

name: Security Without the Feud
description: Iovinus has guarded the frontier for so long that his officers have begun to confuse its safety with their freedom to raid across it. He will seek a settlement that protects Eyrie without requiring Erie's submission. The muster must be honest, the family must be allowed to speak, and the safeguards must bind both commands. His army will defend the country. It will not answer a failed conference by conquering the neighbour.

name: The Men Behind the Numbers
description: A name on a muster roll may represent a soldier, a discharged veteran or an absence nobody has dared to explain. Iovinus must decide who will ask the questions. Local representatives will want to account for the men their villages sent; an army commission will insist that the inquiry remains a matter of service. Either must begin by counting those who are actually there.

name: Montague's Crossing
description: Montague Eyrie, Earl of Verenia, wants to visit Rosaline Erie of Bantry. His officers see a route through hostile positions; he sees the journey to someone whose company he has missed. Iovinus can secure his passage without dictating its purpose. Let the two speak for themselves. A family connection may open the way to an agreement, but it must not become a marriage imposed to spare the dukes an awkward conversation.

name: Stand Down the Raiding Parties
description: The muster has been examined, Montague has opened a personal way across the divide, and the safeguards are ready. Iovinus can now order his officers to put away the excuses by which every raid becomes a precaution. The same restraint will bind Erie. This armistice is the foundation of a permanent settlement, not a year's holiday from the feud.

name: Roads Between the Houses
description: The engineers have spent years marking bridges for demolition. Now they must discover which can carry ordinary traffic again. Survey the approaches, compare the available materials and make the frontier routes usable without an army preparing their passage. The same practical knowledge will serve our own roads and the settlement we are building with Erie.

name: Safeguards That Bind Us Too
description: The muster tells Iovinus what his army can do. Montague's journey reminds him that not every crossing must be an operation. Before concluding an armistice, he must decide what will make its promises credible: mixed patrols empowered to question both commands, or a restitution fund that acknowledges damage and hears property claims. Either course asks the duke to restrain his own supporters. Only then can he ask the same of Vincent.

name: Friendship with Safeguards
description: An open crossing has made the frontier's old habits harder to defend. The treaty will end the official rivalry and relinquish the territorial demands that let either House call its neighbour's independence a provocation. Iovinus retains his army and his government. He gains a peace that no longer needs the prospect of victory to justify itself.

name: Where Command Ends
description: A reliable army needs a clear account of what it may demand from the country it protects. Local councils want a voice when a requisition takes away their last wagon. The officers answer that a command cannot negotiate every order with a village meeting. Iovinus must establish who will hear an objection, and whose duty it will be to make the army respect the answer.
